q1: SELECT A.PROJECT_ID, ROUND(AVG(B.EXPERIENCE_YEARS), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM PROJECT AS A INNER JOIN EMPLOYEE AS B ON A.EMPLOYEE_ID = B.EMPLOYEE_ID GROUP BY A.PROJECT_ID
q2: SELECT SUB.PROJECT_ID, ROUND(SUB.EXPERIENCE/SUB.EMPLOYEES,2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM (SELECT P.PROJECT_ID, COUNT(P.EMPLOYEE_ID) AS EMPLOYEES, SUM(E.EXPERIENCE_YEARS) AS EXPERIENCE FROM PROJECT P JOIN EMPLOYEE E ON P.EMPLOYEE_ID = E.EMPLOYEE_ID GROUP BY P.PROJECT_ID) AS SUB GROUP BY SUB.PROJECT_ID

q2_prompt_sql: SELECT SUB.PROJECT_ID, ROUND(SUB.EXPERIENCE/SUB.EMPLOYEES,2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM (SELECT P.PROJECT_ID, COUNT(P.EMPLOYEE_ID) AS EMPLOYEES, SUM(E.EXPERIENCE_YEARS) AS EXPERIENCE FROM PROJECT P JOIN EMPLOYEE E ON P.EMPLOYEE_ID = E.EMPLOYEE_ID GROUP BY P.PROJECT_ID) AS SUB GROUP BY SUB.PROJECT_ID

explanation: Q1 computes the average experience per project using AVG(B.EXPERIENCE_YEARS) directly. Q2 computes the average experience per project using SUM(EXPERIENCE_YEARS) / COUNT(EMPLOYEE_ID). These should be equivalent in theory, but due to potential integer division in Q2 (before rounding), they may differ if SUM and COUNT produce different rounding behavior compared to AVG.
counterexample_dsp: A project with 3 employees having experience years 1, 2, and 3. Q1 computes 2.00, Q2 computes 2.00, but if one of the experience years is a float or the division yields a different rounding behavior, discrepancy may appear. To ensure clear difference, use small integer values to show rounding behavior.
